items.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
items.summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
items.content:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

items.title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
items.summary: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
items.content:
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

items.title: NINLIVE: The Nine Inch Nails live archive
items.summary: Article URL: https://ninlive.com/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50583274 Points: 337 # Comments: 95
items.content:
Explore shows, download recordings, stream audio, and follow the tape trail across every era. Fan run, not affiliated with the band.

Besides a database driven site. The second most requested feature for ninlive is streaming capability. The future is now. TJ has been working hard behind the scenes to make it happen. You are now able to stream all of your favorite NIN live recordings from 1988-2026. I can't believe how far the site has come in the last year. Some truly incredible work. Login with your discord account and you can save your favorite recordings to stream and keep your faves organized. As always, feedback is always welcome. Reach out via email if you have comments/suggestions about it.

I am currently adding all of the ticket stubs, setlist scans, passes that I have for each show. Please get in contact if you have anything to contribute. I am also looking for photos from past shows. If you are a photographer and would like to contribute some highlights, I'd love to add them to the archive with a link directed to your site of choice.

Other than that. A few tapes trickling in and I do have some that I am slowly working on. None that are insane upgrades. But would need some work and comparison of previous versions. Notably, I have a 1st gen cassette of the 07/12/1991 NOLA Tipitina's show that sounds killer. I recently transferred the elusive collection of acc123456 and have a queue of VHS/Cassette transfers to check over. I also just finished a 200 DAT tape project for a fellow taper out of NYC. The transfer backlog is clear, for the first time in a while. So if you need anything transferred, or have some old NIN hanging around that isn't on the archive. Email us!

items.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis
items.summary: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in the key city of Taiz, cut off from the outside world for weeks.
items.content:
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."

"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.

War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.

Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.

An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.

Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."

Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.

They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.

He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.

"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."

We have not been able to independently verify these figures.

He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.

On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.

The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.

That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.

He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".

Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.

They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.

They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.

Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.

Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.

Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.

"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."

He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.

But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".

The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.

"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."

But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.

"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."

The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."

Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.

Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.

"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.

His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.

"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."

As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.

"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."

On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged

items.title: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for future post-Brexit relations
items.summary: The BBC's political and Europe editors analyse the new agreements between the UK and EU.
items.content:
The United Kingdom and European Union reached a deal on Friday strengthening post-Brexit ties following a summit in Brussels.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, while European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

The BBC's political editor Chris Mason and Europe editor Katya Adler analyse the new agreement and what it could mean for future relations between the UK and EU.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

items.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
items.summary: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.
items.content:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

items.title: Inkling 2 Mini
items.summary: Article URL: https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50581260 Points: 1285 # Comments: 263
items.content:
Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

We’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

Most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.

Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

While looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying the variable-loop model , we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and WorldVQA.

Inkling 2 Mini overcomes the knowledge gap by efficiently using search and tools. It leads open-weights models of similar size on BrowseComp, DeepSearchQA, and MCP Atlas. It is also strong on knowledge work benchmarks that incorporate search and tool use.

Researchers at Stanford measure intelligence per joule: how much energy an LLM needs per query to reach a given level of performance. Researchers at Stanford’s Hazy Research Lab and Scaling Intelligence Lab got early testing access to Inkling 2 Mini. Inkling 2 Mini scored 0.703 running on NVIDIA DGX Spark, significantly higher than other models: 0.430 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 0.159 for Gemma-4-26B-A4B and 0.036 for Qwen3.5-27B. Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI , Saad-Falcon and Narayan et al., 2025 Inkling 2 Mini ran on NVIDIA DGX Spark (128GB) at MXFP8 precision with low reasoning effort in this experiment. The other models ran at NVFP4 (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) and INT4 (Qwen3.5-27B).

Efficiency combined with performance makes Inkling 2 Mini a strong choice for running multiple persistent agents on local hardware. All 20 residents of the energy-conscious village of Thinkyville are managed by Inkling 2 Mini running on a single offline MacBook.

Inkling 2 Mini is not the strongest small model for multi-turn chat or for instructions with many constraints: it scores 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints v1.1, behind Qwen3.8-27B on both. It also trails larger models on reasoning-intensive benchmarks such as CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.

Inkling 2 Mini is a 24-layer model derived from our mainline predictive scaling ladder. The main changes from the mainline recipe were pruning two-thirds of the experts to reduce the model’s size and the introduction of looping to improve reasoning. The rest of training, including quantization and the data mix, followed our mainline recipe.

Inkling 2 Mini has 24 layers, divided into four blocks of six layers each. The two middle blocks run three times, while the first and last blocks each run once. This design builds on prior work on looped transformers and is motivated by the intuition that the middle layers of the model carry more abstract reasoning, while the first and last few layers devote more space to translating between embeddings and internal representations. Universal Transformers , Dehghani et al., 2018 In our experiments, looping the middle 12 layers resulted in larger gains in accuracy than looping the last 12 on 27 out of 28 different evaluations.

Our model uses attention residuals. Attention Residuals , Kimi Team: Guangyu Chen et al., 2026 Instead of adding every layer’s output into one running sum, each layer reads the outputs of the earlier blocks and learns its own mix of them. This allows richer information to pass between loops. Every pass starts with the output of the prelude (the first block). The second and third passes through the middle blocks also read the middle blocks’ outputs from the previous pass, which we call the message.

The previous loop’s message is merged with the prelude’s output via a gate that scales these along with the output of the previous layers in the block. This gate is learned during training: it initially blocks the entire message—which makes each loop start the same as in a non-looping model—and increases the gain on the message over time. This allows us to introduce looping during training in a stable manner.

To evaluate the impact of looping, we compared an unpruned looping version to the unpruned non-looping model on our scaling ladder. The non-looping model cost 7.5% less compute to train, but required 140% more inference compute to match the looped version’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces.

Inkling 2 Mini was trained with 4-bit precision, which we describe in a recent article on Connectionism . We use 4-bit NVFP4 precision in the expert layers on all forward passes from pretraining through RL, bolstered by a dedicated kernel and hardware-accelerated on NVIDIA’s GB300 platform. The final 4 layers’ forward passes ran in 8-bit (MXFP8).

Inkling 2 Mini’s weights are deployed in the same numeric precision they were trained on—20 layers in NVFP4 and 4 in MXFP8—so there is no conversion loss from quantization.

Inkling 2 Mini started training with a sparsity of 48, with 8 experts being chosen out of 384. At a single point during midtraining, we pruned two-thirds of the experts, leaving the 128 experts that were most used in each layer. This was done to cut the total parameter count of the model, allowing it to run faster and on local hardware.

After pruning, the model trained on 1T tokens distilled from a larger internal Inkling model. This step recovered the performance the model had before pruning by training the remaining experts to take over the work of the ones that were deleted.

Following pruning and healing, Inkling 2 Mini underwent SFT with a similar data mix to Inkling 2 Small. This was followed by an RL that totaled 2.2T tokens over 2,000 steps. The post-training phase included on-policy distillation for training alignment, same as Inkling 2 Small.

A key tool for understanding and overseeing an AI system is monitoring its chain of thought (CoT), the reasoning a model writes out as it works through a problem. The usefulness of CoT monitoring stems in part from the standard non-looped transformer architecture, in which each token passes through a fixed stack of layers once. This limits the number of sequential steps of computation the model can perform before it must output a token, so reasoning that needs more steps has to be carried out in generated text, where it can be read.

Looping a transformer’s layers raises this limit. By running the same layers multiple times, looped models increase their serial depth without adding more parameters, meaning that they do more computation per token internally before verbalizing their thought processes via CoT. Reasoning that never appears in the CoT can’t be caught by a CoT monitor, which has led to concerns that looped transformers could be harder to oversee.

items.title: Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
items.summary: Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.
items.content:
A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.

India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019.

He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.

Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.

Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.

At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.

Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs said that Yadav is no longer employed , external by the Indian government.

The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson said.

Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.

Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".

"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."

Indian man admits plot to kill US-based Sikh separatist leader

India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.

Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.

In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun said the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism.

"I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.

Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.

Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.

The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."

items.title: È diventata definitiva la condanna all’ergastolo di Gabriele Bianchi, tra i responsabili dell’omicidio di Willy Monteiro Duarte
items.content:
La Corte di Cassazione ha confermato la condanna all’ergastolo per Gabriele Bianchi, uno dei quattro aggressori di Willy Monteiro Duarte, ucciso con calci e pugni a 21 anni nel settembre del 2020 a Colleferro, in provincia di Roma. Nel 2022 Bianchi fu condannato all’ergastolo in primo grado, ma il tribunale d’appello riconobbe attenuanti generiche e ridusse la pena; poi la Cassazione accolse un ricorso della procura e ordinò un secondo processo d’appello , che si concluse con una condanna a 28 anni. A quel punto la procura contestò di nuovo le attenuanti generiche riconosciute dai giudici, e la Cassazione dispose un terzo processo d’appello, in cui a giugno Bianchi fu appunto condannato all’ergastolo.

L’omicidio di Duarte fu molto raccontato e commentato sui media, anche perché avvenne a seguito di un’aggressione violentissima e immotivata, che durò meno di un minuto. Tra i suoi aggressori c’era anche il fratello di Bianchi, Marco, condannato a sua volta all’ergastolo in via definitiva nel novembre del 2025. Gli altri due responsabili dell’omicidio di Duarte, Francesco Belleggia e Mario Pincarelli, erano già stati condannati in via definitiva a 23 e 21 anni di carcere nell’aprile del 2024.

items.title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
items.summary: Related: Levent Alpöge claims proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis [pdf] - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50574968 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50579568 Points: 2336 # Comments: 1117
items.content:
I am at the American Mathematical Society Executive Committee and Board of Trustees meeting now, and about to chair an hours-long meeting, but this is urgent, so I will try to get this out quickly. Alessandro Maria Masullo has a proposed proof of GRH, and Brian Conrad has been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback which is being incorporated, and it is so far looking good to him. It is all human, with no AI. The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft. I hope people quickly check it, formalize, fill any small gaps if they occur. I really hope it works. I have great faith in Brian’s judgement, and Brian has put a lot of thought into checking what Alessandro has done. There is a long story to tell, but right now I want to get the file out. Here it is.

Update about 8 hours later: I’m out of the meetings, and now catching up! Several people have contacted me to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. (Thanks to several mathematicians in particular who were first to let me know.) As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)

items.title: A Poste Italiane sono stati rubati i dati anagrafici di oltre 1.500 clienti
items.summary: Sono stati pubblicati online dopo un attacco informatico e potrebbero essere usati per tentativi di truffa
items.content:
All’inizio della settimana Poste Italiane ha subìto un attacco informatico nel quale sono stati rubati e pubblicati online i dati di 1.561 clienti (un gruppo molto piccolo, rispetto al totale dei clienti dell’azienda). Le schede relative a ciascuna persona possono contenere nome, cognome, sesso, codice fiscale, luogo di nascita, indirizzo di residenza, email, numero di telefono e numero e data di rilascio del documento di identità. Non risultano pubblicate invece password, credenziali di accesso, numeri di conto, numeri di carte di pagamento, chiavi private o codici per apporre firme digitali.

Non sono stati rubati dati sensibili, ma le informazioni sono sufficienti a formare un profilo che potrebbe essere usato per tentativi di furti d’identità o truffe a nome di Poste Italiane. In particolare potrebbero essere usate per tentativi di phishing, una truffa che consiste nell’invio di email con link che, se cliccati, permettono di accedere al dispositivo del destinatario o a dati sensibili.

L’attacco è avvenuto nella notte tra lunedì e martedì e i dati sono stati sottratti dall’archivio del servizio PosteCert Firma Digitale Remota, che permette di firmare documenti online con lo stesso valore legale di una firma autografa e senza hardware.

Sono stati rubati anche certificati, ordini, fatture e per quasi 650 clienti i nomi dei consulenti di portafoglio. Sono tutte informazioni che un potenziale truffatore può utilizzare per rendere la sua truffa più mirata e credibile.

Poste ha confermato la violazione: ha detto di aver avviato verifiche e che dalle prime analisi non risulta che siano state sottratte credenziali o password per i pagamenti. Secondo RansomNews, un osservatorio che monitora e analizza gli attacchi informatici, i dati rubati riguardano persone residenti in tutte le regioni, ma soprattutto in Lombardia, Lazio e Campania.

I dati sono stati pubblicati da un utente chiamato “flex22” su un forum underground, cioè una community online in cui gli utenti si scambiano informazioni e dati rubati attraverso attività illecite.

items.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
items.summary: Article URL: https://manidoraisamy.com/developer-to-architect.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50579331 Points: 547 # Comments: 299
items.content:
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:

In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect[2]. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.

Notes: [1] Ultimately, you have limited resources. Architecture is about trading off some requirement, so that your app can run with limited resources. Take CAP theorem as an example. You have to trade off consistency or availability or partition tolerance for your database. If you don't understand the tradeoff and ask AI to build a database that has all 3, it would reinvent Google Spanner++ and expect Google scale datacenter to run it. [2] This post is trending on HN . Some have correctly pointed out that good developers already do architecture and bad architects propose ivory tower architecture that falls apart during implementation. I have built ivory tower architecture whenever I am handsoff. This will become more common with AI, if we don't debug its code or don't hand code critical parts of the app from time to time. So, don't stop coding, but it's not a full time job either.

items.title: In Italia è stata approvata la guida semiautonoma delle Tesla
items.summary: È un sistema con cui le auto si manovrano da sole sotto una supervisione umana, ma per vederle per strada ci vorrà ancora un po'
items.content:
Il ministero delle Infrastrutture e dei Trasporti italiano ha autorizzato la società di automobili Tesla a usare la tecnologia Tesla Assisted Driving, che permette alle sue auto di svolgere manovre in autonomia, come la navigazione lungo un percorso stabilito, la sterzata, i cambi di corsia e il parcheggio. Questa tecnologia richiede comunque la supervisione di una persona seduta al posto del guidatore, che deve essere pronta a intervenire in caso di problemi e che resta responsabile per le manovre dell’auto. È in sostanza una forma di guida semiautonoma, spesso descritta con l’espressione “hands-off, eyes-on”, ovvero “senza mani e occhi aperti”.

L’autorizzazione rende da subito utilizzabile la tecnologia in Italia, che però non è ancora disponibile: Tesla ha detto che la renderà operativa sulle sue auto attraverso un aggiornamento dei software, ma non ha specificato quando succederà. Ha detto che costerà 99 euro al mese per chi vorrà usarla.

A livello europeo questa tecnologia non è ancora stata approvata (era previsto un voto a ottobre, che però è stato rinviato), ma nel frattempo i singoli stati possono approvarla nel proprio paese con un procedimento che si chiama “omologazione provvisoria”: serve a rendere disponibili nei paesi membri dell’Unione Europea le nuove tecnologie che non sono ancora previste dalle norme comunitarie, in attesa che vengano approvate, cosa che richiede diversi passaggi burocratici.

Hanno fatto per primi quest’omologazione i Paesi Bassi, che poi sono stati seguiti da altri undici paesi, per ultimo l’Italia, che è anche l’unico tra i grandi paesi europei. In sostanza i Paesi Bassi hanno sbrigato le lunghe procedure burocratiche necessarie ad assicurare che la tecnologia fosse sicura, e i paesi arrivati dopo hanno potuto approvare il procedimento già comprovato. Anche il ministro dei Trasporti Matteo Salvini ha parlato di «omologazione provvisoria».

Il sistema di guida semiautonoma di Tesla si basa su otto telecamere che permettono all’auto di avere una visione di 360 gradi. Le informazioni raccolte dalle telecamere vengono poi analizzate dal computer di bordo in tempo reale.

items.title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
items.summary: Article URL: https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/11/20/unforced-euler-singularity-unforced-navier-stokes-singularity-and-the-generalized-riemann-hypothesis/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50578358 Points: 517 # Comments: 225
items.content:
Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao

20 November, 2026 in math.AP , math.NT | Tags: AI , incompressible Euler equations , Levent Alpöge , Matei Coiculescu , Navier-Stokes equations , Riemann hypothesis , Tristan Buckmaster | by Terence Tao

Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are:

See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results.

David Hilbert in 2443: Has someone proved the Riemann Hypothesis?

And why should he be surprised? Riemann perhaps could be, but why Hilbert if formalization of mathematics was his idea, the idea of a “thinking machine” goes back to Leibniz and the theoretical notion of a Turing machine was introduced 7 years before Hilbert’s death? This may be surprising to us, because it happened so quickly, we knew the visions of AI from sci-fi books and at the same time we were aware of the failures of previous approaches to formal theorem proving, but c’mon in 2443?

Hilbert had just awoken from 1943-land, when few if any people believed it was more than a distant dream that a computer could navigate among and occasionally beyond what he surely regarded as some of highest pinnacles of human intellectual depth and creativity. To be told that this had actually occurred, and only eight decades into his five-century sleep, could be seriously unsettling.

(Besides which he was still groggy and getting used to the time change.)

Sure, I am just saying that the very idea that a proof could be done by the machine and the question of whether mechanization of mathematics is possible came from Hilbert, so I am not sure if back in 1943 he would have said “This is never going to happen”. The term “robot” and the exploration of thinking machines in sci-fi literature goes back to the 1920s. So, while surprising at the technical level, the basic idea was already a part of the mathematical and pop-cultural imaginarium, even if not its mainstream.

In 2443, David Hilbert would probably be more surprised that Europe has become uninhabitable because climate change has caused southern Europe to become an extension of the Sahara desert and the AMOC to collapse rendering northern Europe to become like Siberia.

I tried to turn Lean proof into a human readible and beginner friendly manuscript here with the help of AI.

43 Page GRH Proof Outline: https://www.gokhanmergen.com/pubs/grh-reader-guide/GRH_Reader_Friendly_Guide.pdf

Thank you for the ordering by how digested the results are. That ordering is the whole story, and it is worth being explicit about why.

For the first two results the digestion path is already visible: human-readable proof, strategy broadly clear, Lean formalisation on top. A reader can form a judgement in an afternoon. The third has no such path yet. A Lean-only artifact of that size is a different kind of object, and the question “is it right” splits into questions that resolve on very different timescales: does the headline statement in Lean say what we mean by GRH; does the archive compile against a known-good Lean with only standard axioms; is the strategy something a number theorist recognises as a proof. The Zulip thread can answer the second relatively quickly. The third is the one that has always taken years.

The two precedents are both uncomfortable. Wiles announced in 1993, the gap surfaced within months, and the repair took until 1995. Mochizuki published in a refereed journal in 2012 and the people who work on the problem still do not accept it. In neither case could the answer be read off the artifact.

Which makes the interesting question not “is it true” but “what observable event would settle it, and who is entitled to say so”. For anyone trying to price this rather than just follow it, writing that down before the claim exists is the only version that is worth anything. Written afterwards it collapses into an argument about credibility, which is precisely the failure mode this whole episode is about.

Disclosure: I work on https://science.markets , which runs a market on this question. The resolution rule is fixed before the market opens and cannot be edited: https://science.markets/markets/riemann-zeta-critical-line/ — it requires a complete unconditional proof in ZFC, independently checked with no unresolved gap, and it says in advance that finite numerical verification does not count and that independence from ZFC leaves it unresolved. Being forced to write down what does not count was the useful part.

Are we allowed to just advertise gambling sites on this blog now? Next thing you know we’ll see a paper “The DraftKings proof of P != NP”.

By the way, this is an LLM generated comment. This is sort of a classic signature “That ordering is the whole story, and it is worth being explicit about why.” blah blah, worth explicit about why. There’s a couple of more fingerprints here but I’ll leave it as an exercise to the reader to find them.

Perhaps the world has changed in the last 2.5 months, however, I cannot help but remember your warning in early September,

“The point remains that there is a substantial opportunity cost in converting a historically productive and motivating problem (such as Navier-Stokes regularity) into a mere viral social media post advertising some benchmark progress, rather than actually advancing the field and developing the next generation of both problems to ask, and people to work on them.”

It feels like Alpöge’s actions around GRH have seen your fears come to fruition. I cannot help but feel that regardless of our feelings around the use of AI in mathematics we as a math community should not highlight Alpöge’s actions without a healthy dose of criticism.

If something is lean verified I think releasing is a good thing. The community can begin digesting/interpreting or building off of the results more quickly and with great plurality.

Also, if an individual withholds new results because they feel they have greater results upcoming, that’s well within their right, of course that comes at a risk.

Ideally well known vehicles will emerge for triaging huge lean results, and another vehicle that is meant for human consumption.

I think there’s a big difference between Alpoge’s announcement here and OpenAI’s dump from a few months back. Specifically this line:

“I intend to do my best to understand and impart understanding of this argument and its certain simplifications, to speak about it, to write it properly.”

I genuinely think Alpoge does care about mathematics, and this problem in particular, and his motivation was not to drum up PR.

Alpoge might care about this problem, but mainly to the extent that it brings him credit/glory. Otherwise he wouldn’t have dumped this AI slop, but worked to explain it better. His pattern of behavior over the last few months regarding other problems is not that of a person with integrity. At this point, he is basically a child with a new (and very powerful) toy – lots of compute, and powerful internal models, which he’s using to gather as much credit and fame as possible. Any such recognition should take into account the differential in resources between him and mathematicians in academia.

Mathematicians have asked AI companies to not feed big open problems to internal models, and clearly neither the companies nor their employees such as Alpoge give a damn.

Alpoge works for Anthropic and his apparent interest is producing AI generated Lean proofs of Millennium problems. Impossible to know a person’s motivations, but there’s a huge element of PR here.

Of course, positive things to be said about this vs OpenAI dump. (He’s a legitimate mathematician who talks to mathematicians; has clearly been listening to feedback from the community; whole thing less vulgar).

I genuinely believe that Alpoge is not doing this as PR for Anthropic. He is doing it for personal glory-seeking, because he has exclusive access to better technology.

It should be obvious by now that they don’t want anyone to work in anything ever again. To feel any sense of mastery or satisfaction or control ever again. You are supposed to be a happy consumer who claps every time you see another benchmark headline in the news. And they want to be the ones with the dopamin levee. There will be no more math students, no “next generation”.

Does anyone have a rough estimate for how long until the GRH proof is verified?

Lean builds should be finishing up soon with people that have powerful servers, and then it will be checked thoroughly for the next few days. Should be soon where we have a pretty good idea if it’s looking good.

It is also worth linking to this post from Ravi Vakil, about an independent, non-AI proof of GRH from Alessandro Maria Masullo: https://math216.wordpress.com/2026/11/20/hurried-announcement-alessandro-masullo-grh/

The draft is incomplete, it includes footnotes like “Correct statement”, “Insert statement”, “Correct this subsection”, and “Include section”. Hopefully these would be fixed soon.

items.title: Microsoft Teams, addio agli aggiornamenti su iOS e iPadOS 17
items.summary: Da metà dicembre parte il passaggio a iOS e iPadOS 18 per i nuovi aggiornamenti di Teams.
items.content:
Da metà dicembre Microsoft inizierà a togliere il supporto di Teams a iOS 17 e iPadOS 17, e il cambio riguarda i prossimi aggiornamenti dell'app e sarà introdotto in tutto il mondo, con la conclusione prevista per l'inizio di gennaio 2027. Ciò significa che quando l'aggiornamento raggiungerà il proprio dispositivo, il requisito minimo per installare una nuova versione di Teams sarà iOS 18 su iPhone o iPadOS 18 su iPad.

Se sul telefono c'è già Teams, però, a gennaio l'icona continuerà ad aprire l'app. Nell'avviso agli amministratori, identificato come MC1556088 nel Message Center di Microsoft 365, l'azienda dice che continuerà a essere possibile anche fare il login. In pratica si potrà tenere la versione che si sta usando, anche se da quel momento Microsoft non la supporterà più su quei sistemi. La distinzione conta soprattutto per chi legge la notizia e si sta chiedendo se potrà ancora entrare nella prossima riunione dal proprio iPad, ma diciamo con chiarezza che il cambio di requisiti non blocca quell'accesso.

Per verificare se si è coinvolti basta guardare la versione di iOS o iPadOS nelle impostazioni. Se è la 17 e il dispositivo offre un aggiornamento di sistema, si può installarlo prima di tornare nell'App Store a cercare l'aggiornamento di Teams. Per chi usa un iPad che non può superare iPadOS 17, il sistema operativo rimane invece il limite. La versione già presente potrà ancora essere usata, ma l'App Store non potrà installare quelle che richiedono il sistema più recente.

items.title: L'86% delle runner tra 18 e 24 anni è stata molestata, una su sei ha smesso per paura
items.summary: Fiona May: 'Correre è libertà, non un'esercizio di prudenza'
items.content:
L'86% delle ragazze tra i 18 e i 24 anni che corrono all'aperto ha subito almeno una molestia durante la corsa. Lo rileva la prima indagine nazionale sul fenomeno, realizzata da Nielsen per ChangeTheGame e presentata oggi all'Allianz MiCo, nell'ambito della Powerade Milano Half Marathon, alla presenza di Fiona May. "Correre dovrebbe essere un gesto di libertà, non un esercizio continuo di prudenza - dice l'ex atleta - Più vedo questi numeri, più mi arrabbio". Su 5.055 donne di 18-50 anni intervistate, 1.471 sono runner (in Italia se ne stimano circa 3 milioni): il 68% ha subito molestie, l'86% tra le 18-24enni, il 79% tra le 25-34enni e il 57% tra le 35-50enni. Il fenomeno riguarda tutto il Paese: 73% al Centro, 69% nel Nord Est, 66% nel Nord Ovest, 65% al Sud e nelle Isole.

Circa due runner su tre temono molestie prima ancora di uscire. Tra le ex runner, una su sei ha smesso di correre all'aperto per insicurezza o molestie: il 44% per episodi ripetuti, il 38% per un clima di insicurezza, il 18% per un singolo episodio grave.

"Quando il 96% delle runner che hanno subito molestie dichiara di adottare almeno una precauzione per sentirsi più sicura, è evidente che il problema non può essere lasciato alla responsabilità delle singole donne - aggiunge Fiona May -. Cambiare percorso, rinunciare alla musica, modificare gli orari o condividere la propria posizione è il prezzo che troppe donne sono costrette a pagare per poter semplicemente correre. La sicurezza non deve limitare la libertà di scegliere dove e quando correre: deve essere una responsabilità collettiva".

items.title: Cos’è Avio e perché è importante
items.summary: L'azienda italiana che si occupa di Spazio e difesa potrebbe essere comprata dai finlandesi, ma in mezzo c'è il governo
items.content:
Il ministro della Difesa Guido Crosetto ha detto che il governo potrebbe ostacolare o bloccare il tentativo della società finlandese Iceye di comprare Avio, azienda italiana specializzata in sistemi di lancio nello Spazio. Avio ha competenze molto specifiche e richieste nel settore aerospaziale, e recentemente è diventata rilevante anche per il settore della difesa. La notizia dell’operazione ha agitato più che altro il governo italiano, essendo Avio meno nota ai non addetti ai lavori.

Avio ha sede a Colleferro, in provincia di Roma, ha più di 1.500 dipendenti e dal 2017 è quotata alla borsa di Milano. Negli ultimi due anni il prezzo delle sue azioni è più che triplicato e agli attuali valori di borsa l’intera azienda vale quasi 2 miliardi di euro.

Nello specifico Avio si occupa di propulsione e sistemi di lancio, cioè di tutto quello che serve per portare cose nello Spazio. Avio progetta e costruisce i Vega, una famiglia di lanciatori europei, cioè dei razzi, per portare nello Spazio satelliti di piccole e medie dimensioni, come quelli che osservano la Terra, controllano il clima o servono alla difesa.

Avio è l’azienda responsabile dell’intero programma Vega: progetta e produce i razzi a Colleferro e poi li spedisce nella Guyana francese, dove si trova il centro spaziale europeo da cui partono. Recentemente ha cominciato a vendere anche i servizi di lancio, di cui prima si occupava solo l’azienda francese Arianespace. Quindi ora non costruisce soltanto i razzi per portare satelliti nello Spazio: ce li porta anche.

Avio produce anche alcuni sistemi di propulsione di Ariane 6, cioè il modello europeo di razzo che serve a portare nello Spazio i satelliti più pesanti.

Vega e Ariane 6 sono i due principali modelli di razzi progettati e costruiti in territorio europeo, senza i quali l’Unione Europea dovrebbe rifornirsi da aziende straniere, come la statunitense SpaceX, di Elon Musk: è successo per esempio tra il 2022 e il 2024, quando dovette affidarsi ai servizi di SpaceX a causa di alcuni problemi tecnici e ritardi sui suoi lanciatori.

Contribuendo allo sviluppo e alla costruzione di entrambi i lanciatori europei, Avio è quindi un’azienda essenziale per l’autonomia delle attività spaziali europee in un momento in cui la collaborazione con gli Stati Uniti non è più scontata.

L’officina di Avio a Colleferro, che il Post ha visitato nel 2022 (Tommaso Merighi/Il Post)

Avio è considerata un’azienda sensibile anche dal punto di vista della difesa. I satelliti fanno parte dell’infrastruttura militare, e garantiscono attività di comunicazioni, osservazione e navigazione. Se n’è vista recentemente l’importanza: la dipendenza dell’Ucraina dai servizi dai satelliti di Starlink , il servizio di SpaceX, l’ha messa in una posizione difficile a ottobre, quando l’azienda statunitense ne ha limitato l’uso da parte dei droni militari ucraini, una decisione che secondo il governo ucraino era una probabile ritorsione del governo di Donald Trump.

Non è però solo una questione di satelliti. Con le guerre in corso la domanda di armamenti e missili è aumentata molto, ed è così che è cresciuta una parte fino a poco tempo fa marginale degli affari di Avio: produce anche i sistemi di propulsione per i missili, un settore molto specifico, di nicchia, eppure essenziale per il funzionamento di questi armamenti.

Non ci sono molti produttori con questa competenza e per questo il giro d’affari di Avio nella difesa è in forte crescita. Sta anche costruendo una fabbrica in Virginia, negli Stati Uniti, che produrrà per conto di Lockheed Martin e Raytheon, due dei maggiori produttori di armamenti al mondo. In Europa lavora soprattutto per la difesa aerea, cioè per i sistemi che servono ad abbattere aerei, droni e missili. Il cliente principale è MBDA, il consorzio europeo dei missili.

Tutte queste peculiarità hanno reso Avio molto interessante per Iceye, l’azienda finlandese che vuole comprarla: Iceye è specializzata in tecnologie satellitari, e ha detto di voler acquisire Avio per ottenere un accesso più stabile ai servizi di lancio.

Ha quindi avviato un’OPA, un’offerta pubblica di acquisto, cioè una delle diverse modalità con cui si possono comprare società quotate in borsa. Nel comunicato stampa sull’offerta ha scritto che si propone di creare un grande gruppo europeo del settore aerospaziale e di mantenere l’attuale forza lavoro, gli impegni e gli investimenti fatti da Avio in Italia, paese che secondo Iceye resterebbe comunque «il centro delle attività di lancio e propulsione».

L’officina di Avio a Colleferro, che il Post ha visitato nel 2022 (Tommaso Merighi/Il Post)

Iceye si propone di comprare le azioni di Avio al prezzo di 41 euro l’una, con un premio di più del 20 per cento rispetto ai valori di mercato e per un valore di 2,05 miliardi di euro. L’obiettivo di Iceye è l’acquisizione del 100 per cento di Avio e il cosiddetto delisting , cioè la rimozione dalla borsa. Iceye considererà riuscita l’operazione se otterrà almeno i due terzi delle azioni: è una quota che consente infatti di prendere in autonomia anche le decisioni più importanti.

La prima è che il socio più importante di Avio è Leonardo, la più rilevante società italiana nel settore della difesa e tra le maggiori a livello europeo. Leonardo possiede una quota del 18 per cento ed è plausibile che non voglia vendere, visti i recenti progressi nello sviluppo e nella produzione di sistemi di propulsione per i missili.

La seconda è che può mettersi di mezzo il governo italiano. Crosetto ha detto che il governo potrebbe attivare il cosiddetto golden power : lo strumento previsto dalla legge con cui la presidenza del Consiglio può ostacolare o persino bloccare tentativi di acquisizione di società italiane in settori ritenuti particolarmente strategici o coinvolti nella sicurezza nazionale. L’aerospazio e soprattutto la difesa sono tra questi.

Prima di poter eventualmente attivare il golden power il governo deve però aspettare che Iceye notifichi formalmente i termini dell’operazione alla presidenza del Consiglio, cosa che ancora non è avvenuta.

items.title: I'm quite pleased by the tech architecture of my art website
items.summary: Article URL: https://klauria.tech/klauria-art/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50577991 Points: 94 # Comments: 18
items.content:
It is a truth universally acknowledged, that every developer blog begins by explaining the new static site generator they wrote to make it. This post isn’t exactly that, but maybe only on a technicality, in that it’s not about this website…

Earlier this year I decided to put a some of my paintings and sketchbook pages online. I don’t much use social media besides Hacker News, but I wanted to share my work with friends and family. So I’d been sending scans of my work in group chats. That was fine for a bit but so messy and disorganized. Sometimes someone asked, “Where did you paint this?” Sometimes a friend wanted to see what it looked like in real life. My little brother suggested a map with a marker for each piece. That was a good idea! For that I’d need a website and some code. Here, take a look at the map, its done now! You can zoom and click on markers to see the painting!

When it comes to tech side projects there are two wolves inside me. One is the Wolf of Pragmatism, which wants to smash every problem with whatever hammer is nearest at hand: “Isn’t this just some trivial React? Dump the images in S3 and call it a day. This website is for friends and family; you have no traffic to speak of. Put a CDN in front so your parents in India get reasonable performance.”

The other is the Aesthetic Wolf: “This should be a static website. The content almost never changes.”

Yes. This is a static website. I do at most four, and on average less than 0.3, paintings a day. The content almost never changes. Why should javascript render the page on the user’s browser? Why should any code even run on the server? I should have the bytes for every page just sitting there, ready to be shipped. The correct server implementation for this problem is open followed by sendfile inside the event loop (I’m joking but only kind of?). The Aesthetic Wolf won.

But the problem with a static website is that for every new post, I need to add a file, and run a build, and deploy it to production. I made a hundred paintings this year! Even if I automate a lot of it, I wanted a better UI for stuff like adding tags and setting location. And the best UI for what’s essentially a CRUD app is … probably a web UI. But if I have a web UI that changes the content of the website, that’s not a static website any more.

So what I really want is a website that’s static for everyone else, but dynamic for me. I want a build system but I want it triggered by actions in a nice CRUD UI that I make, not GitHub actions or a terminal.

Here’s my silly little solution to this silly conundrum. I’m sure the design I’m about to describe isn’t novel, but I did come up with it. I’m just pleased by it because it’s an efficient solution to the exact problem I happened to have. It’s dollar-efficient for me, i.e., it’s free*. It’s resource-efficient for Cloudflare, because the static assets are rarely rebuilt and mostly sit there cached. And it’s fast, because the bytes are mostly sitting there in a CDN waiting to be sent.

(Asterisk: the compute and bandwidth are free. The storage is currently free, but if I paint enough then I’ll go past the 10 GB free tier and pay a couple cents per month.)

The main idea is that every html page is rendered on the server, but with a cache header telling Cloudflare’s infrastructure to cache the response forever (well, for 30 days). Then, whenever I upload a new art piece or change the set of tags or anything like that, the request handler for this write operation invalidates all cached pages. That’s it.

There’s one detail that makes this work well for an image-heavy website: we generate several smaller sizes of each image at upload time , and I actually do it on the client’s browser. Since I’m the only uploader, that would be my browser. We need the smaller sizes for thumbnails and cards, where sending the full archival images would be way too slow. Those downsampled images are uploaded along with originals to Cloudflare’s R2, their S3-equivalent.

Why downsample at upload time? Cloudflare does offer an image service that’ll do the resizing the first time you make a request for that image at that size, and it’ll cache that resized copy. But in my case I already know the three sizes I want, so it’s faster to just precompute and store them. The additional storage doesn’t add up to much, because the archival images are enormous compared to downsampled copies.

All the metadata for all pieces goes in a single json file that also lives in R2. When someone requests a dynamic html page, like the one for pieces tagged #summer , a piece of code runs in a Cloudflare worker. It reads the json and generates the html, which is then cached until the next invalidation. Cloudflare’s CDN handles the rest: if someone in India later requests the same page, the cached artifact is sent to an edge machine in India and cached there for a while. I suppose Cloudflare can choose to rerun the worker instead of copying the artifact, which is fine by me. Based on my testing that’s not what happens: the generator writes a timestamp on each page so I can see when it was generated.

The website has some interactive stuff like maps and timelines. Those are just embedded javascript that run on the client’s browser and read that single metadata json file to initialize. They don’t write anything back to the server, so there’s no database or anything. They’re just displaying the information in different ways. For example, here’s an interactive timeline of my pieces over the years. I haven’t uploaded everything I’ve ever made, so this is biased toward recent stuff.

(To be very technically correct, this timeline component doesn’t read the json directly. Its bars are drawn on the server, and it gets a per-month list derived from the metadata to handle clicking and paging.)

Here’s what the page for a piece looks like. The metadata json has the information to figure out what pieces were done nearby and around the same time, so I show all that. This is an embedded iframe so you can scroll and click:

This is where Pragmatic Wolf won. Here’s the possible optimization: whenever I make an edit, we should invalidate only those pages that are potentially affected by that edit. A good build system certainly works this way: when you change one file, it recompiles only those artifacts that (transitively) depend on it.

In my case, however, dependencies aren’t explicitly written down anywhere. The code to generate a page just runs, and potentially any change in the metadata json could cause its output to be different. I could try to encode the dependencies for each page and component, but it’s so easy to get this wrong and introduce bugs in the future. The result is a half-updated website, i.e., a correctness bug.

So while it’s true that adding a new piece only changes the #evening page if the new piece actually has that tag, I considered it too tricky to get this cache invalidation right, and decided to just invalidate everything. If I were using a normal static site generator then the CDN could potentially do this optimization by noticing that the hash of an artifact hasn’t changed, so it doesn’t need to be updated on every edge machine.

Anyway here is a waterfall in Washington, the one in Twin Peaks apparently:

And here’s the view from right outside my house in Brooklyn:

By the way, the specific javascript framework I ended up using is called Astro. Cloudflare bought them so they’re pretty nicely integrated. But you don’t really need it for this, you could write your own code to run in the Worker to generate the page. The whole trick is in some careful management of cache.

items.title: La pioggia non è finita
items.summary: Sono attese altre tre perturbazioni. Le aree più esposte sono quelle tirreniche, in particolare a ridosso dei rilievi Leggi
items.content:
A partire dalla seconda settimana di novembre l’intenso flusso d’aria che scorre in alta quota ( corrente a getto ) si è spostato decisamente verso sud, trasportando nel Mediterraneo le famiglie di perturbazioni tipiche delle latitudini più settentrionali. Quando le correnti provengono in maniera così diretta dall’Atlantico, le regioni più esposte alle piogge sono quelle tirreniche, in particolare a ridosso dei rilievi.

Dal 9 novembre nell’alta Toscana e sull’Appennino tosco-emiliano si sono registrati quantitativi di pioggia elevatissimi: più di 900 millimetri in undici giorni nella stazione di Fornovolasco in Garfagnana, più della pioggia che cade a Firenze in un anno intero.

In questa situazione, diventa evidente il ruolo del grande trasporto di vapore acqueo ( fiume atmosferico ) dai caldi oceani subtropicali, che contribuisce a rendere le precipitazioni particolarmente abbondanti insieme alle alte temperature dei mari, tuttora da record.

Le piogge hanno provocato piene notevoli dei fiumi e saturato i terreni appenninici, favorendo grosse frane che hanno isolato interi paesi. Il problema è che la pioggia non è finita.

Domenica 22 novembre è attesa una nuova perturbazione, seguita da altre due, giovedì 26 e domenica 29. La situazione in quelle zone potrebbe quindi diventare critica. Bisognerà seguire le allerte emesse dai centri funzionali regionali e le comunicazioni dei comuni.

Le piogge saranno quindi abbondanti e superiori alla media del periodo. Le temperature medie settimanali saranno ancora molto superiori alla norma, soprattutto al centro-sud.

Gradi centigradi in più o in meno rispetto alla media stagionale degli ultimi vent’anni. Elaborazione dati: European centre for medium-range weather forecasts (Ecmwf).

Millimetri di pioggia in più o in meno rispetto alla media stagionale degli ultimi vent’anni. Elaborazione dati: European centre for medium-range weather forecasts (Ecmwf).

Internazionale pubblica ogni settimana una pagina di lettere. Ci piacerebbe sapere cosa pensi di questo articolo. Scrivici a: posta@internazionale.it
